details:
You can't be friends with everyone

VRChat needs a friendship meter, the more you hang out with that one person, the higher you grow, it should balance out with everyone on your list. Acquainted, Mutual, Friends and Besties. You can't be Besties with everyone on you list, but you can be Acquainted with everyone.

The Core Concept

I propose adding a Dynamic Friendship Meter to the social system. Instead of a binary "Friend" or "Favorite" status, the system should track interaction frequency and duration to automatically assign relationship tiers. This creates a more organic social graph that reflects actual usage rather than just who we clicked "Add" on once.

Proposed Tiers

The system should categorize contacts into four distinct levels based on shared time and interaction:

Acquainted: The default state for anyone on your friends list whom you rarely interact with. This clears the clutter of old contacts without requiring mass unfriending.

Mutual: Users you interact with occasionally or share common social circles with.

Friends: Regular hangout partners. This tier is reached after consistent interaction over time.

Besties: The highest tier, reserved for the people you spend the most time with. Crucially, this slot should be limited. You cannot be "Besties" with 200 people; the meter must balance out, forcing the system to highlight your actual closest connections. 

How It Works

Passive Tracking: The meter increases based on time spent in the same instance, voice proximity, and active interaction.

Decay: If you stop hanging out with someone, their level slowly decays over time, moving from "Bestie" back down to "Friend" or "Acquainted."

Visual Indicators: Distinct icons or colors on nameplates and the friend list to instantly recognize how close you are to someone. 

Why This Is Needed

Currently, the friends list is often bloated with hundreds of people we met once and never saw again, making it hard to find who is actually available and close to us. As noted in community discussions, many users struggle with "friend list lag" and the difficulty of distinguishing close friends from casual contacts. 

This system solves several issues:

Social Clutter: It automatically organizes your list based on reality, not just a past friend request.

Meaningful Connections: It gamifies socializing in a healthy way, encouraging users to nurture specific relationships to maintain "Bestie" status.

Privacy & Boundaries: It helps users identify who they are actually close to versus who is just a "contact," aiding in decisions about who to set to "Invite Only" or "Ask Me" status.

Privacy Considerations

Given the community's valid concerns about stalking and privacy regarding mutual friends, this feature must include robust privacy controls:

Opt-Out: Users must be able to hide their specific tier status from others.

Visibility Settings: Options to show tiers only to "Friends," "Friends of Friends," or "No One."

No "Guilt by Association": The data should be personal to the user. Just because I consider User A a "Bestie" doesn't mean User A's other friends can see that unless settings allow it. 

This feature would modernize how we manage social capital in VRChat, making the platform feel more like a living community and less like a static contact list.

Mitigating Social Drama & Harassment

A major barrier to cleaning up friend lists is the fear of interpersonal conflict. Users often retain hundreds of inactive contacts to avoid the awkwardness or hostility of being unfriended. 

How the Meter Solves This:

Passive vs. Active Rejection: Currently, cleaning a list requires active removal, which sends a notification (or is immediately visible) to the other user, often interpreted as a personal slight. The Friendship Meter relies on passive decay. If two people stop hanging out, the status naturally drops from "Bestie" to "Friend" to "Acquainted" over time without any button press. This removes the "breakup" moment that triggers drama.

Objective Justification: It is harder to argue with a system than a person. If a user asks, "Why am I not your Bestie anymore?", the answer is simply, "We haven't hung out in a while," rather than "I didn't want you on my list." This shifts the blame from personal rejection to natural social drift.

Reduced Cross-Platform Harassment: Many users report being harassed on Discord after being unfriended in VRChat. By automating the demotion of casual contacts, users can maintain a clean, organized list without ever triggering the notification that leads to these confrontations.

Trust Rank Safety: Community discussions highlight that mass-unfriending can negatively impact a user's Trust Rank (deranking them from Trusted to Known).  A passive system avoids this penalty entirely, as you aren't technically "removing" people, just letting the relationship tier adjust based on activity. 

This approach allows users to curate their inner circle safely, protecting their mental health and privacy without inviting real-world conflict.
title: Friendship Meter
